extracted.intended_audience: Philippine IP practitioners, rights-holders, in-house counsel and litigators
extracted.subtask_description: Practical procedural and substantive standards for enforcing, defending and challenging intellectual property rights in the Philippines under the IP Code and the 2020 Revised Rules of Procedure for IP Cases, including administrative remedies, courts, evidence, remedies and timelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction for civil IPR cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil Intellectual Property Rights cases (IPR cases) are within the jurisdiction of the Regional Trial Court designated by the Supreme Court as Special Commercial Courts under the 2020 Revised Rules of Procedure for IP Cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special Commercial Courts follow venue rules in civil cases; administrative remedies may be available elsewhere (e.g., Bureau of Legal Affairs) depending on the remedy sought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commencing a civil IPR action and key procedural timelines
rubrics_metrics.description: A civil IPR case is commenced by filing a verified Complaint; summons must be served within five (5) days of receipt by the court; defendant must file an Answer within 30 calendar days from service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-trial is conducted to simplify issues; if trial is necessary, hearings begin within 60 calendar days from termination of pre-trial and completed not later than 60 calendar days from the date of initial trial. Parties have up to 30 days to present witnesses on scheduled dates; failure to present a witness on scheduled date = waiver. Court may require memoranda/draft decisions within a non-extendible 30 days; court shall render judgment within 60 calendar days after submission. Unless restrained, judgments are executory even pending appeal; appeals to Court of Appeals via Rule 43.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commencing a criminal IPR action and criminal timelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Criminal IPR cases start with filing at the Department of Justice or Office of the Prosecutor via a preliminary investigation; an information is filed with the trial court after a verified complaint and prima facie finding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge evaluates information for probable cause and may dismiss or issue warrant/commitment. After acquiring jurisdiction, arraignment and pre-trial must terminate within 30 calendar days; parties referred to mediation on civil aspect for non-extendible 30 days. Trials are conducted expeditiously; each party has 60 calendar days to present evidence-in-chief on agreed trial dates. Judgment promulgated within 60 calendar days from submission. Appeals under Rule 122.

rubrics_metrics.name: Customs enforcement mechanisms (Bureau of Customs IPRD)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Bureau of Customs maintains a permanent Intellectual Property Rights Division (IPRD) and an IPR Registry where holders may record their IPR; Customs may conduct random inspections and issue Alert or Hold Orders on shipments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IPR holder may request Alert/Hold Orders. If inspection shows no basis for seizure, the Alert/Hold is immediately lifted. Otherwise, matter referred to Collector of Customs for issuance of a Warrant of Seizure and Detention and possible seizure proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fee waivers for geographical indications and criminal cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Geographical Indication Rules provide that for geographical indications filed by indigenous cultural communities/indigenous peoples, filing fees may be waived, fully or partially. There is no filing fee for criminal cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory pre-litigation / mediation for certain administrative IP complaints
rubrics_metrics.description: Under IPOPHL Memorandum Circular No. 2020-047 (as amended), administrative complaints for violations of IPR and/or unfair competition, Inter Partes cases, technology transfer payment disputes, certain license disputes and certain appeals must undergo pre-litigation or mandatory mediation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inter Partes cases are submitted to Bureau of Legal Affairs-Alternative Dispute Resolution Services (BLA-ADRS) for mandatory mediation, conducted online/virtual unless parties opt for face-to-face. Each party pays a non-refundable Php4,000.00 (USD69.00).

rubrics_metrics.name: Arbitration as a dispute resolution option
rubrics_metrics.description: Arbitration is mandatory only when parties are governed by an arbitration agreement that stipulates arbitration as the preferred or sole method of dispute resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no special IP arbitration procedure in the Philippines; IP arbitration is governed by the general arbitration law applicable to the parties' agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard/quantum of proof in IP cases
rubrics_metrics.description: For civil IPR cases, the quantum of evidence is preponderance of evidence; for criminal IPR cases, proof beyond reasonable doubt is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Rules of Court apply suppletorily; certain statutory presumptions in the IP Code and the 2020 Revised Rules affect evidentiary burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof in patent cases and exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally the burden to substantiate patent infringement rests on the party alleging infringement, subject to statutory and case-law exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exception example: where the subject matter is a process for obtaining a product and the product is new or identical products likely made by the process, the burden may shift to the alleged infringer to prove a different process was used (Smith Kline Beckman).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent infringement tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Two tests used by the Supreme Court to determine patent infringement: (1) literal infringement and (2) the doctrine of equivalents (Philips Seafood v. Tuna Processors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark registration presumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: A certificate of registration of a mark is prima facie evidence of: (1) validity of the registration, (2) ownership by the registrant, and (3) exclusive right to use the mark in connection with the goods/services specified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This presumption affects proof obligations in trademark infringement and unfair competition cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test for likelihood of confusion (dominancy test)
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine likelihood of confusion, the dominancy test is used: focus on similarity of the prevalent features of competing trademarks which might cause confusion or deception (UFC Philippines Inc v. Fiesta Barrio Manufacturing Corporation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actual confusion or absolute certainty of confusion is not required to protect registered trademarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of intent to defraud in unfair competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Intent to defraud or deceive the public is presumed in unfair competition when: (1) defendant passes off a product using imitative devices/signs which mislead buyers; (2) defendant makes false statements in trade to discredit another's goods/business; (3) similarity of packaging/offering is so striking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright ownership and subsistence presumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Ownership of copyright is presumed to belong to a complainant if claimed through affidavit evidence under Section 218 of the IP Code; copyright is presumed to subsist in a work if the defendant does not put subsistence in issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere registration/deposit with the National Library or IPO does not itself carry the presumption of ownership by the registrant/depositor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court-appointed assessors and expert committees for technical issues
rubrics_metrics.description: For patent cases, the court may appoint two or more assessors to provide scientific/technical knowledge; the court may also order a committee of three (each party nominates an expert; court appoints the third from a list).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court may act motu proprio or upon motion. The court can request IPOPHL assistance (equipment, technical facilities, personnel) for highly technical matters. Rule 128, Section 52 allows presentation of expert witnesses after qualification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of discovery and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: The Rules of Court on discovery apply suppletorily to IP cases. Parties may avail of discovery modes not later than thirty (30) days from joinder of issues in civil IPR actions, including interrogatories, requests for admissions, and production/inspection of documents or things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requests for discovery may be objected to within ten (10) days on limited grounds: manifestly incompetent/immaterial/irrelevant; privileged/undisclosed information; or for harassment. Compliance must be made within ten (10) days from receipt or from notice of court ruling. Administrative IP complaints may move for depositions upon written interrogatories after answer filed. A deposition of a witness abroad must be taken within six (6) months from order allowing it, subject to exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-examination and types of administrative proceedings without trial
rubrics_metrics.description: Information and evidence in civil/criminal/IPV cases may be subject to cross-examination by the opposing party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certain administrative/Inter Partes cases are decided on affidavits and pleadings without trial and thus typically lack cross-examination opportunities: (i) oppositions to trademark/service mark registrations; (ii) petitions to cancel trademark/service mark registrations; (iii) petitions to cancel invention patents, utility model, industrial design registrations, claims or topography/layout registrations; and (iv) petitions for Compulsory Licensing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defenses to patent infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Available defenses include showing patent invalidity on grounds that the invention is not new or patentable, insufficient disclosure, or contrary to public order/morality; prior user defense; government-authorized use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good faith is not a defense unless claiming prior user status under Sections 73 or 159 or when specific damages provisions apply (Sections 76, 156, 216).

rubrics_metrics.name: Defenses to trademark infringement and unfair competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademark defenses include that the mark is non-registrable (generic, customary, descriptive), prior user in good faith, statutory allowances for certain imported/off-patent drugs, and doctrine of unrelated goods. Unfair competition defense may be absence of fraud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law examples cited (Zuneca Pharmaceutical v. Natrapharm; Taiwan Kolin v. Kolin Electronics; Shang Properties v. St. Francis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Defenses to trade secrets disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Defenses include that the information is widely known outside employer’s business, known to employees/others, owner did not take ample measures to guard secrecy, or information readily obtainable independently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employee accused may argue management’s determination of confidentiality lacks factual basis (Air Philippines v. Pennswell).

rubrics_metrics.name: Defenses to copyright infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Defenses include subject matter not protectible, statutory fair use exceptions under Section 184.1, or satisfying the four factors of fair use under Section 185 of the IP Code.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may challenge each IP right
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent: the person who made the invention but is not the patent applicant may assert rights; any interested person may petition to cancel a patent or claim better right. Trademark: any person who believes they would be damaged may oppose an application or petition for cancellation; cancellation may be filed by any person believing they are or will be damaged. Copyright: anyone sued or threatened with suit may challenge extent or existence of asserted copyright. Geographical Indication: any interested person may file third-party observation or seek revocation on enumerated grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grounds for challenges vary by right (see other entries).

rubrics_metrics.name: When challenges may be made
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent: certain court actions must be filed within one year from publication of the patent application (changed from three years); cancellation period for patents is not specified. Trademark: opposition within 30 days from publication; cancellation generally within five years from registration though some grounds may be raised at any time. Copyright: defenses/challenges may be raised at any time during existence of copyright. Geographical Indication: third-party observation within one month from publication; revocation may be sought any time a ground arises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forum and procedure for challenging rights; grounds of invalidity
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent actions involving inventors or true inventors are instituted before Regional Trial Courts designated as Special Commercial Courts; cancellations may be before Bureau of Legal Affairs unless highly technical and then heard by committee of three. Trademark oppositions/cancellations are before Bureau of Legal Affairs as Inter Partes cases; unfair competition, criminal and administrative remedies also available. Copyright challenges depend on whether matter is civil, criminal or administrative. Geographical Indication matters filed with Director of Bureau of Trademarks (Registrar).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grounds of invalidity generally mirror statutory grounds discussed earlier (novelty, patentability, sufficiency of disclosure, genericness, fraud, lack of effective control for GI, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Other methods to remove or limit IP rights (agreements and declaratory relief)
rubrics_metrics.description: IP rights may be affected by private agreements including licensing and assignment; parties can file declaratory relief actions to obtain judicial declarations of rights, duties, or obligations or petitions to reform agreements under Civil Code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent law expressly allows a patent holder to surrender his patent for cancellation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies for patent infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentee or any person possessing right/title/interest may file civil action for damages and litigation expenses and apply for injunctive writs; court may order disposal of infringing goods/materials/implements without compensation; repeated infringement after final judgment may attract criminal liability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note: one who is not a patent holder generally may not file an action for infringement (except as otherwise provided by statute).

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies for trademark infringement and special remedies for well-known marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Registered mark owner may recover damages (may be doubled if actual intent to mislead), request impounding of sales invoices/documents, injunctive writs, delivery/destruction of infringing goods without compensation, and injunctions against future printing/publication by innocent printers/publishers in certain circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative remedies via Bureau of Legal Affairs include fines, damages assessments and provisional remedies (TRO, preliminary injunction, preliminary attachment). Owner may oppose or petition to cancel infringer registrations. For well-known marks not registered in the Philippines, remedies (opposition, cancellation, unfair competition action) may be available under conditions; if well-known mark is registered, broader remedies available even if goods/services are not identical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies for trade secrets violations
rubrics_metrics.description: Owner may file criminal cases for revealing secrets with abuse of office (Article 291 RPC) or revelation of industrial secrets (Article 292 RPC); injunctions to prevent disclosure by one who obtained information in confidence or through confidential relationship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other statutes (e.g., National Revenue Code provisions) may impose sanctions for divulging confidential information by government officers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies for copyright infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright holder may seek injunctive writs, damages (actual or just/temperate) or statutory damages before judgment, impounding of sales invoices/documents, destruction of infringing copies/devices without compensation, and may bring criminal or administrative actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs of enforcement and fee recovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Costs depend on the type of action elected by the IPR holder; for ordinary civil actions for damages, the IPR holder pays necessary filing fees, which depend on the amount of damages claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No single fixed schedule provided here; other court rules and fee schedules determine exact costs. Recovery of costs may depend on the forum and claims for litigation expenses/damages.
